A strange word to come from Christ's mouth, and at this time surprising, for it comes in the midst of divers pleasing prospects, in which, one would think, he should have said, Now is my soul <hi type="italic">pleased.</hi> Note, Trouble of soul sometimes follows after great enlargements of spirit. In this world of mixture and change we must expect damps upon our joy, and the highest degree of comfort to be the next degree to trouble. When Paul had been in the third heavens, he had a <hi type="italic">thorn in the flesh.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen27856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27857" type="x-p"/> 1. Christ's dread of his approaching sufferings: <hi type="italic">Now is my soul troubled.</hi> Now the black and dismal scene began, now were the first throes of the travail of his soul, now his agony began, his soul <hi type="italic">began to be exceedingly sorrowful.</hi> Note, (1.) The sin of our soul was the trouble of Christ's soul, when he undertook to redeem and save us, and to make his soul an offering for our sin. (2.) The trouble of his soul was designed to ease the trouble of our souls; for, after this, he said to his disciples (<reference osisRef="John.14.1">ch. xiv. 1</reference>), "<hi type="italic">Let not your hearts be troubled;</hi> why should yours be troubled and mine too?" Our Lord Jesus went on cheerfully in his work, in prospect of the joy set before him, and yet submitted to a trouble of soul. Holy mourning is consistent with spiritual joy, and the way to eternal joy. Christ was <hi type="italic">now</hi> troubled, now in sorrow, now in fear, now for a season; but it would not be so always, it would not be so long. The same is the comfort of Christians in their troubles; they are but <hi type="italic">for a moment,</hi> and will be turned into joy. <div eID="gen27857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27858" type="x-p"/> 2. The strait he seems to be in hereupon, intimated in those words, <hi type="italic">And what shall I say?</hi> This does not imply his consulting with any other, as if he needed advice, but considering with himself what was fit to be said now. When our souls are troubled we must take heed of speaking unadvisedly, but debate with ourselves what we shall say. Christ speaks like one at a loss, as if what he should choose he wot not. There was a struggle between the work he had taken upon him, which required sufferings, and the nature he had taken upon him, which dreaded them; between these two he here pauses with, <hi type="italic">What shall I say?</hi> He looked, and there was <hi type="italic">none to help,</hi> which put him to a stand. Calvin observes this as a great instance of Christ's humiliation, that he should speak thus like one at a loss. <hi type="italic">Quo se magis exinanivit gloriæ Dominus, eo luculentius habemus erga nos amoris specimen—The more entirely the Lord of glory emptied himself, the brighter is the proof of the love he bore us.</hi> Thus he was <hi type="italic">in all points tempted like as we are,</hi> to encourage us, when we know not what to do, to direct our eyes to him. <div eID="gen27858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27859" type="x-p"/> 3. His prayer to God in this strait: <hi type="italic">Father, save me from this hour,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ek tes oras tautes</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">out of this hour,</hi> praying, not so much that it might not come as that he might be brought through it. <hi type="italic">Save me from this hour;</hi> this was the language of innocent nature, and its feelings poured forth in prayer. Note, It is the duty and interest of troubled souls to have recourse to God by faithful and fervent prayer, and in prayer to eye him as a Father. Christ was voluntary in his sufferings, and yet prayed to be saved from them. Note, Prayer against a trouble may very well consist with patience under it and submission to the will of God in it. Observe, He calls his suffering <hi type="italic">this hour,</hi> meaning the expected events of the time now at hand. Hereby he intimates that the time of his suffering was, (1.) A set time, set to an hour, and he knew it. It was said twice before that his hour was not yet come, but it was now so near that he might say it was come. (2.) A short time. An hour is soon over, so were Christ's sufferings; he could see through them to the <hi type="italic">joy set before him.</hi> <div eID="gen27859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27860" type="x-p"/> 4. His acquiescence in his Father's will, notwithstanding. He presently corrects himself, and, as it were, recalls what he had said: <hi type="italic">But for this cause came I to this hour.</hi> Innocent nature got the first word, but divine wisdom and love got the last. Note, those who would proceed regularly must go upon second thoughts. The complainant speaks first; but, if we would judge righteously, we must hear the other side. With the second thought he checked himself: <hi type="italic">For this cause came I to this hour;</hi> he does not silence himself with this, that he could not avoid it, there was no remedy; but satisfies himself with this, that he would not avoid it, for it was pursuant to his own voluntary engagement, and was to be the crown of his whole undertaking; should he now fly off, this would frustrate all that had been done hitherto. Reference is here had to the divine counsels concerning his sufferings, by virtue of which it behoved him thus to submit and suffer. Note, This should reconcile us to the darkest hours of our lives, that we were all along designed for them; see <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1 Thess. iii. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen27860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27861" type="x-p"/> 5. His regard to his Father's honour herein. Upon the withdrawing of his former petition, he presents another, which he will abide by: <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name,</hi> to the same purport with <hi type="italic">Father, thy will be done;</hi> for God's will is for his own glory. This expresses more than barely a submission to the will of God; it is a consecration of his sufferings to the glory of God. It was a mediatorial word, and was spoken by him as our surety, who had undertaken to satisfy divine justice for our sin. The wrong which by sin we have done to God is in his glory, his declarative glory; for in nothing else are we capable of doing him injury. We were never able to make him satisfaction for this wrong done him, nor any creature for us; nothing therefore remained but that God should get him honour upon us in our utter ruin. Here therefore our Lord Jesus interposed, undertook to satisfy God's injured honour, and he did it by his humiliation; he denied himself in, and divested himself of, the honours due to the Son of God incarnate, and submitted to the greatest reproach. Now here he makes a tender of this satisfaction as an equivalent: "<hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name;</hi> let thy justice be honoured upon the sacrifice, not upon the sinner; let the debt be levied upon me, I am solvent, the principal is not." Thus he <hi type="italic">restored that which he took not away.</hi> <div eID="gen27861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27862" type="x-p"/> II. The Father's answer to this address; for he heard him always, and does still. Observe, 1. How this answer was given. By a voice from heaven. The Jews speak much of a <hi type="italic">Bath-k&#244;l—the daughter of a voice,</hi> as one of those divers manners by which God in time past spoke to the prophets; but we do not find any instance of his speaking thus to any but to our Lord Jesus; it was an honour reserved for him (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Matt. iii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.17.5">xvii. 5</reference>), and here, probably, this audible voice was introduced by some visible appearance, either of light or darkness, for both have been used as vehicles of the divine glory. 2. What the answer was. It was an express return to that petition, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify thy name: I have glorified it</hi> already, and <hi type="italic">I will glorify it yet again.</hi> When we pray as we are taught, <hi type="italic">Our Father, hallowed be thy name,</hi> this is a comfort to us, that is it an answered prayer; answered to Christ here, and in him to all true believers. (1.) The name of God had been glorified in the life of Christ, in his doctrine and miracles, and all the examples he gave of holiness and goodness. (2.) It should be further glorified in the death and sufferings of Christ. His wisdom and power, his justice and holiness, his truth and goodness, were greatly glorified; the demands of a broken law were fully answered; the affront done to God's government satisfied for; and God accepted the satisfaction, and declared himself well pleased. What God has done for the glorifying of his own name is an encouragement to us to expect what he will yet further do. He that has secured the interests of his own glory will still secure them. <div eID="gen27862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27863" type="x-p"/> III. The opinion of the standers-by concerning this voice, <reference osisRef="John.12.29">v. 29</reference>. We may hope there were some among them whose minds were so well prepared to receive a divine revelation that they understood what was said and bore record of it. But notice is here taken of the perverse suggestion of the multitude: some of them said that <hi type="italic">it thundered:</hi> others, who took notice that there was plainly an articulate intelligible voice, said that certainly <hi type="italic">an angel spoke to him.</hi> Now this shows, 1. That it was a real thing, even in the judgment of those that were not at all well affected to him. 2. That they were loth to admit so plain a proof of Christ's divine mission. They would rather say that it was this, or that, or any thing, than that God spoke to him in answer to his prayer; and yet, if it thundered with articulate sounds (as <reference osisRef="Rev.10.3-Rev.10.4">Rev. x. 3, 4</reference>), was not that God's voice? Or, if angels spoke to him, are not they God's messengers? But thus <hi type="italic">God speaks once, yea twice, and man perceives it not.</hi> <div eID="gen27863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27864" type="x-p"/> IV. The account which our Saviour himself gives of this voice. <div eID="gen27864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27865" type="x-p"/> 1. Why it was sent (<reference osisRef="John.12.30">v. 30</reference>): "It came <hi type="italic">not because of me,</hi> not merely for my encouragement and satisfaction" (then it might have been whispered in his ear privately), "<hi type="italic">but for your sakes.</hi>" (1.) "That all you who heard it may <hi type="italic">believe that the Father hath sent me.</hi>" What is said from heaven concerning our Lord Jesus, and the glorifying of the Father in him, is said for our sakes, that we may be brought to submit to him and rest upon him. (2.) "That you my disciples, who are to follow me in sufferings, may therein be comforted with the same comforts that carry me on." Let this encourage them to part with life itself for his sake, if they be called to it, that it will redound to the honour of God. Note, The promises and supports granted to our Lord Jesus in his sufferings were intended for our sakes. <hi type="italic">For our sakes</hi> he <hi type="italic">sanctified himself,</hi> and <hi type="italic">comforted himself.</hi> <div eID="gen27865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27866" type="x-p"/> 2. What was the meaning of it. He that lay in the Father's bosom knew his voice, and what was the meaning of it; and two things God intended when he said that he would <hi type="italic">glorify his own name:</hi>— <div eID="gen27866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27867" type="x-p"/> (1.) That by the death of Christ Satan should be conquered (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now is the judgment.</hi> He speaks with a divine exultation and triumph. "Now the year of my redeemed is come, and the time prefixed for breaking the serpent's head, and giving a total rent to the powers of darkness; now for that glorious achievement: <hi type="italic">now, now,</hi> that great work is to be done which has been so long thought of in the divine counsels, so long talked of in the written word, which has been so much the hope of saints and the dread of devils." The matter of the triumph is, [1.] That <hi type="italic">now is the judgment of the world;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">krisis</hi></hi>, take it as a medical term: "Now is the <hi type="italic">crisis</hi> of this world." The sick and diseased world is now upon the turning point; this is the critical day upon which the trembling scale will turn for life or death, to all mankind; all that are not recovered by this will be left helpless and hopeless. Or, rather, it is a law term, as we take it: "Now, judgment is entered, in order to the taking out of execution against the prince of this world." Note, The death of Christ was the <hi type="italic">judgment of this world. First,</hi> It is a judgment of discovery and distinction—<hi type="italic">judicium discretionis;</hi> so Austin. Now is the trial of this world, for men shall have their character according as the cross of Christ is to them; to some it is foolishness and a stumbling-block, to others it is the wisdom and power of God; of which there was a figure in the two thieves that were crucified with him. By this men are judged, what they think of the death of Christ. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is a judgment of favour and absolution to the chosen ones that are in the world. Christ upon the cross interposed between a righteous God and a guilty world as a sacrifice for sin and a surety for sinners, so that when he was judged, and <hi type="italic">iniquity laid upon him,</hi> and he was wounded for our transgressions, it was as it were the judgment of this world, for an everlasting righteousness was thereby brought in, not for Jews only, but the whole world, <reference osisRef="1John.2.1-1John.2.2">1 John ii. 1, 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is a judgment of condemnation given against the powers of darkness; see <reference osisRef="John.16.11">ch. xvi. 11</reference>. Judgment is put for vindication and deliverance, the asserting of an invaded right. At the death of Christ there was a famous trial between Christ and Satan, the serpent and the promised seed; the trial was for the world, and the lordship of it; the devil had long borne sway among the children of men, time out of mind; he now pleads prescription, grounding his claim also upon the forfeiture incurred by sin. We find him willing to have come to a composition (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.6-Luke.4.7">Luke iv. 6, 7</reference>); he would have given the kingdoms of this world to Christ, provided he would hold them by, from, and under him. But Christ would try it out with; by dying he takes off the forfeiture to divine justice, and then fairly disputes the title, and recovers it in the court of heaven. Satan's dominion is declared to be a usurpation, and the world adjudged to the Lord Jesus as his right, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">8</reference>. The judgment of this world is, that it belongs to Christ, and not to Satan; to Christ therefore let us all <hi type="italic">atturn</hi> tenants. [2.] That <hi type="italic">now is the prince of this world cast out. First,</hi> It is the devil that is here called the <hi type="italic">prince of this world,</hi> because he rules over the men of the world by the things of the world; he is the <hi type="italic">ruler of the darkness of this world,</hi> that is, of this dark world, of those in it that <hi type="italic">walk in darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2 Cor. iv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.12">Eph. iv. 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is said to be <hi type="italic">cast out,</hi> to be <hi type="italic">now</hi> cast out; for, whatever had been done hitherto towards the weakening of the devil's kingdom was done in the virtue of a Christ to come, and therefore is said to be done <hi type="italic">now.</hi> Christ, reconciling the world to God by the merit of his death, broke the power of death, and cast out Satan as a destroyer; Christ, reducing the world to God by the doctrine of his cross, broke the power of sin, and cast out Satan as a deceiver. The bruising of his heel was the breaking of the serpent's head, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. When his oracles were silenced, his temples forsaken, his idols famished, and the kingdoms of the world became Christ's kingdoms, then was the <hi type="italic">prince of the world cast out,</hi> as appears by comparing this with John's vision (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.8-Rev.12.11">Rev. xii. 8-11</reference>), where it is said to be done by the <hi type="italic">blood of the Lamb.</hi> Christ's frequent casting of devils out of the bodies of people was an indication of the great design of his whole undertaking. Observe, With what assurance Christ here speaks of the victory over Satan; it is as good as done, and even when he yields to death he triumphs over it. <div eID="gen27867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27868" type="x-p"/> (2.) That by the death of Christ souls should be converted, and this would be the casting out of Satan (<reference osisRef="John.12.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">If I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all men unto me.</hi> Here observe two things:— <div eID="gen27868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27869" type="x-p"/> [1.] The great design of our Lord Jesus, which was to <hi type="italic">draw all men to him,</hi> not the Jews only, who had been long in a profession a people <hi type="italic">near to God,</hi> but the Gentiles also, who had been <hi type="italic">afar off;</hi> for he was to be the <hi type="italic">desire of all nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.7">Hag. ii. 7</reference>), and <hi type="italic">to him must the gathering of the people be.</hi> That which his enemies dreaded was that the world would go after him; and he would draw them to him, notwithstanding their opposition. Observe here how Christ himself is all in all in the conversion of a soul. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is Christ that draws: I <hi type="italic">will draw.</hi> It is sometimes ascribed to the Father (<reference osisRef="John.6.44">ch. vi. 44</reference>), but here to the Son, who is the <hi type="italic">arm of the Lord.</hi> He does not drive by force, but draws with the <hi type="italic">cords of a man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Hos. xi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer. xxxi. 3</reference>), draws as the loadstone; the soul is <hi type="italic">made willing,</hi> but it is in a <hi type="italic">day of power. Secondly,</hi> It is to Christ that we are drawn: "I will draw them to me as the centre of their unity." The soul that was at a distance from Christ is brought into an acquaintance with him, he that was shy and distrustful of him is brought to love him and trust in him,—drawn up to his terms, into his arms. Christ was now going to heaven, and he would draw men's hearts to him thither. <div eID="gen27869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27870" type="x-p"/> [2.] The strange method he took to accomplish his design by <hi type="italic">being lifted up from the earth.</hi> What he meant by this, to prevent mistake, we are told (<reference osisRef="John.12.33">v. 33</reference>): <hi type="italic">This he spoke signifying by what death he should die,</hi> the death of the cross, though they had designed and attempted to stone him to death. He that was crucified was first nailed to the cross, and then lifted up upon it. He was <hi type="italic">lifted up as a spectacle to the world;</hi> lifted up between heaven and earth, as unworthy of either; yet the word here used signifies an honourable advancement, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ean hypsotho</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">If I be exalted;</hi> he reckoned his sufferings his honour. Whatever death we die, if we die in Christ we shall be lifted up out of this dungeon, this den of lions, into the regions of light and love. We should learn of our Master to speak of dying with a holy pleasantness, and to say, "We shall then be lifted up." Now Christ's drawing all men to him followed his being <hi type="italic">lifted up from the earth. First,</hi> It followed after it in time. The great increase of the church was after the death of Christ; while Christ lived, we read of thousands at a sermon miraculously fed, but after his death we read of thousands at a sermon added to the church. Israel began to multiply in Egypt after the death of Joseph. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It followed upon it as a blessed consequence of it. Note, There is a powerful virtue and efficacy in the death of Christ to draw souls to him. The cross of Christ, though to some a <hi type="italic">stumbling-stone,</hi> is to others a <hi type="italic">loadstone.</hi> Some make it an allusion to the drawing of fish into a net; the lifting up of Christ was as the spreading of the net (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.47-Matt.13.48">Matt. xiii. 47, 48</reference>); or to the setting up of a standard, which draws soldiers together; or, rather, it refers to the lifting up of the brazen serpent in the wilderness, which drew all those to it who were stung with fiery serpents, as soon as ever it was known that it was lifted up, and there was healing virtue in it. O what flocking was there to it! So there was to Christ, when salvation through him was preached to all nations; see <reference osisRef="John.3.14-John.3.15">ch. iii. 14, 15</reference>. Perhaps it has some reference to the posture in which Christ was crucified, with his arms stretched out, to invite all to him, and embrace all that come. Those that put Christ to that ignominious death thought thereby to drive all men from him; but the devil was outshot in his own bow. <hi type="italic">Out of the eater came forth meat.</hi> <div eID="gen27870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27871" type="x-p"/> V. The people's exception against what he said, and their cavil at it, <reference osisRef="John.12.34">v. 34</reference>. Though they had heard the voice from heaven, and the gracious words that proceeded out of his mouth, yet they object, and pick quarrels with him. Christ had called himself the <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.23">v. 23</reference>), which they knew to be one of the titles of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan. vii. 13</reference>. He had also said that the <hi type="italic">Son of man must be lifted up,</hi> which they understood of his dying, and probably he explained himself so, and some think he repeated what he said to Nicodemus (<reference osisRef="John.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">So must the Son of man be lifted up.</hi> Now against this, <div eID="gen27871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27872" type="x-p"/> 1. They alleged those scriptures of the Old Testament which speak of the perpetuity of the Messiah, that he should be so far from being cut off in the midst of his days that he should be a <hi type="italic">priest for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Ps. cx. 4</reference>), and a king <hi type="italic">for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Ps. lxxxix. 29</reference>, &c.), that he should have <hi type="italic">length of days for ever and ever,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his years as many generations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.4">Ps. xxi. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.6">lxi. 6</reference>), from all which they inferred that the Messiah should not die. Thus great knowledge in the letter of the scripture, if the heart be unsanctified, is capable of being abused to serve the cause of infidelity, and to fight against Christianity with its own weapons. Their perverseness in opposing this to what Jesus had said will appear if we consider, (1.) That, when they vouched the scripture to prove that the Messiah <hi type="italic">abideth for ever,</hi> they took no notice of those texts which speak of the Messiah's death and sufferings: they had heard out of the law that <hi type="italic">Messiah abideth for ever;</hi> and had they never heard out of the law that Messiah should <hi type="italic">be cut off</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Dan. ix. 26</reference>), and that he should <hi type="italic">pour out his soul unto death</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa. liii. 12</reference>), and particularly that his <hi type="italic">hands and feet</hi> should be pierced? Why then do they make so strange of the <hi type="italic">lifting up of the Son of man?</hi> Note, We often run into great mistakes, and then defend them with scripture arguments, by putting those things asunder which God in his word has put together, and opposing one truth under pretence of supporting another. We have heard out of the gospel that which exalts free grace, we have heard also that which enjoins duty, and we just cordially embrace both, and not separate them, nor set them at variance. (2.) That, when they opposed what Christ said concerning the sufferings of the Son of man, they took no notice of what he had said concerning his glory and exaltation. They had heard out of the law that <hi type="italic">Christ abideth for ever;</hi> and had they not heard our Lord Jesus say that he should be glorified, that he should bring forth much fruit, and draw all men to him? Had he not just now promised immortal honours to his followers, which supposed his abiding for ever? But this they overlooked. Thus unfair disputants oppose some parts of the opinion of an adversary, to which, if they would but take it entire, they could not but subscribe; and in the doctrine of Christ there are paradoxes, which to men of corrupt minds are stones of stumbling—as Christ <hi type="italic">crucified,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">glorified; lifted up from the earth,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">drawing all men to him.</hi> <div eID="gen27872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27873" type="x-p"/> 2. They asked hereupon, <hi type="italic">Who is the Son of man?</hi> This they asked, not with a desire to be instructed, but tauntingly and insultingly, as if now they had baffled him, and run him down. "Thou sayest, <hi type="italic">The Son of man must die;</hi> we have proved the Messiah must not, and where is then thy Messiahship? This Son of man, as thou callest thyself, cannot be the Messiah, thou must therefore think of something else to pretend to." Now that which prejudiced them against Christ was his meanness and poverty; they would rather have no Christ than a suffering one. <div eID="gen27873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27874" type="x-p"/> VI. What Christ said to this exception, or rather what he said <hi type="italic">upon it.</hi> The objection was a perfect cavil; they might, if they pleased, answer it themselves: man dies, and yet is immortal, and abideth for ever, so the <hi type="italic">Son of man.</hi> Therefore, instead of answering these fools according to their folly, he gives them a serious caution to take heed of trifling away the day of their opportunities in such vain and fruitless cavils as these (<reference osisRef="John.12.35-John.12.36">v. 35, 36</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Yet a little while,</hi> and but a little while, <hi type="italic">is the light with you;</hi> therefore be wise for yourselves, and <hi type="italic">walk while you have the light.</hi>" <div eID="gen27874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27875" type="x-p"/> 1. In general, we may observe here, (1.) The concern Christ has for the souls of men, and his desire of their welfare. With what tenderness does he here admonish those to look well to themselves who were contriving ill against him! Even when he <hi type="italic">endured the contradiction of sinners,</hi> he sought their conversion. See <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Prov. xxix. 10</reference>. (2.) The method he takes with these objectors, <hi type="italic">with meekness instructing those that opposed themselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2 Tim. ii. 25</reference>. Were but men's consciences awakened with a due concern about their everlasting state, and did they consider how little time they have to spend, and none to spare, they would not waste precious thoughts and time in trifling cavils. <div eID="gen27875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27876" type="x-p"/> 2. Particularly we have here, <div eID="gen27876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27877" type="x-p"/> (1.) The advantage they enjoyed in having Christ and his gospel among them, with the shortness and uncertainty of their enjoyment of it: <hi type="italic">Yet a little while is the light with you.</hi> Christ is this light; and some of the ancients suggest that, in calling himself the light, he gives a tacit answer to their objection. His dying upon the cross was as consistent with his <hi type="italic">abiding for ever</hi> as the setting of the sun every night is with his perpetuity. The duration of Christ's kingdom is compared to that of the sun and moon, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.17">Ps. lxxii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.36-Ps.89.37">lxxxix. 36, 37</reference>. The ordinances of heaven are unchangeably fixed, and yet the sun and moon set and are eclipsed; so Christ the Sun of righteousness abides for ever, and yet was eclipsed by his sufferings, and was but a little while within our horizon. Now, [1.] The Jews at this time had the <hi type="italic">light with them;</hi> they had Christ's bodily presence, heard his preaching, saw his miracles. The scripture is to us a light shining in a dark place. [2.] It was to be but a little while with them; Christ would shortly leave them, their visible church state would soon after be dissolved and the kingdom of God taken from them, and blindness and hardness would happen unto Israel. Note, It is good for us all to consider what a little while we are to have the light with us. Time is short, and perhaps opportunity not so long. The candlestick may be removed; at least, we must be removed shortly. Yet a little while is the light of life with us; yet a little while is the light of the gospel with us, the day of grace, the means of grace, the Spirit of grace, yet a very little while. <div eID="gen27877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27878" type="x-p"/> (2.) The warning given them to make the best of this privilege while they enjoyed it, because of the danger they were in of losing it: <hi type="italic">Walk while you have the light;</hi> as travellers who make the best of their way forward, that they may not be benighted in their journey, because travelling in the night is uncomfortable and unsafe. "Come," say they, "let us mend our pace, and get forward, while we have day-light." Thus wise should we be for our souls who are journeying towards eternity. Note, [1.] It is our business to walk, to press forward towards heaven, and to get nearer to it by being made fitter for it. Our life is but a day, and we have a day's journey to go. [2.] The best time of walking is while we have the light. The day is the proper season for work, as the night is for rest. The proper time for getting grace is when we have the word of grace preached to us, and the Spirit of grace striving with us, and therefore then is the time to be busy. [3.] We are highly concerned thus to improve our opportunities, for fear lest our day be finished before we have finished our day's work and our day's journey: "<hi type="italic">Lest darkness come upon you,</hi> lest you lose your opportunities, and can neither recover them nor despatch the business you have to do without them." Then <hi type="italic">darkness</hi> comes, that is, such an utter incapacity to make sure the great salvation as renders the state of the careless sinner quite deplorable; so that, if his work be undone then, it is likely to be undone for ever. <div eID="gen27878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27879" type="x-p"/> (3.) The sad condition of those who have sinned away the gospel, and are come to the period of their day of grace. <hi type="italic">They walk in darkness,</hi> and know neither <hi type="italic">where</hi> they go, nor <hi type="italic">whither</hi> they go; neither the way they are walking in, nor the end they are walking towards. He that is destitute of the light of the gospel, and is not acquainted with its discoveries and directions, wanders endlessly in mistakes and errors, and a thousand crooked paths, and is not aware of it. Set aside the instructions of the Christian doctrine, and we know little of the difference between good and evil. He is going to destruction, and knows not his danger, for he is either sleeping or dancing at the pit's brink. <div eID="gen27879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27880" type="x-p"/> (4.) The great duty and interest of every one of us inferred from all this (<reference osisRef="John.12.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">While you have light, believe in the light.</hi> The Jews had now Christ's presence with them, let them improve it; afterwards they had the first offers of the gospel made to them by the apostles wherever they came; now this is an admonition to them not to out-stand their market, but to accept the offer when it was made to them: the same Christ saith to all who enjoy the gospel. Note, [1.] It is the duty of every one of us <hi type="italic">to believe in the gospel light,</hi> to receive it as a divine light, to subscribe to the truths it discovers, for it is a light to our eyes, and to follow its guidance, for it is a light to our feet. Christ is the light, and we must believe in him as he is revealed to us; as a true light that will not deceive us, a sure light that will not misguide us. [2.] We are concerned to do this while we have the light, to lay hold on Christ while we have the gospel to show us the way to him and direct us in that way. [3.] Those that believe in the light <hi type="italic">shall be the children of light;</hi> they shall be owned as <hi type="italic">Christians,</hi> who are called <hi type="italic">children of light</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.8">Luke xvi. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Eph. v. 8</reference>) and of the day, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5">1 Thess. v. 5</reference>. Those that have God for their Father are children of light, for God is light; they are born from above, and heirs of heaven, and children of light, for heaven is light. <div eID="gen27880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27881" type="x-p"/> VII. Christ's retiring from them, hereupon: <hi type="italic">These things spoke Jesus,</hi> and said no more at this time, but left this to their consideration, <hi type="italic">and departed, and did hide himself from them.</hi> And this he did, 1. For their conviction and awakening. If they will not regard what he hath said, he will have nothing more to say to them. They are joined to their infidelity, as Ephraim to idols; <hi type="italic">let them alone.</hi> Note, Christ justly removes the means of grace from those that quarrel with him, and <hi type="italic">hides his face</hi> from <hi type="italic">a froward generation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.20">Deut. xxxii. 20</reference>. 2. For his own preservation. He hid himself from their rage and fury, retreating, it is probable, to Bethany, where he lodged. By this it appears that what he said irritated and exasperated them, and they were made worse by that which should have made them better.
entries.766c5f8d3b746a2ead5b9606606079457e2817b4: <div eID="gen27881" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Unbelief of the People.</title> <div sID="gen27882" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> But though he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not on him: <hi type="super">38</hi> That the saying of Esaias the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spake, Lord, who hath believed our report? and to whom hath the arm of the Lord been revealed? <hi type="super">39</hi> Therefore they could not believe, because that Esaias said again, <hi type="super">40</hi> He hath blinded their eyes, and hardened their heart; that they should not see with <hi type="italic">their</hi> eyes, nor understand with <hi type="italic">their</hi> heart, and be converted, and I should heal them. <hi type="super">41</hi> These things said Esaias, when he saw his glory, and spake of him. <div eID="gen27882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27883" type="x-p"/> We have here the honour done to our Lord Jesus by the Old-Testament prophets, who foretold and lamented the infidelity of the many that believed not on him. It was indeed a dishonour and grief to Christ that his doctrine met with so little acceptance and so much opposition; but <hi type="italic">this</hi> takes off the wonder and reproach, makes the offence of it to cease, and made it no disappointment to Christ, that herein the scriptures were fulfilled. Two things are here said concerning this untractable people, and both were foretold by the evangelical prophet Isaiah, that they <hi type="italic">did not</hi> believe, and that they <hi type="italic">could not</hi> believe. <div eID="gen27883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27884" type="x-p"/> I. They did not believe (<reference osisRef="John.12.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Though he had done so many miracles before them,</hi> which, one would think, should have convinced them, yet they believed not, but opposed him. Observe, <div eID="gen27884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27885" type="x-p"/> 1. The abundance of the means of conviction which Christ afforded them: He <hi type="italic">did miracles, so many miracles;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tosauta semeia</hi></hi> signifying both so many and so great. This refers to all the miracles he had wrought formerly; nay, the blind and lame now came to him into the temple, and he healed them, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.14">Matt. xxi. 14</reference>. His miracles were the great proof of his mission, and on the evidence of them he relied. Two things concerning them he here insists upon:—(1.) The number of them; they were <hi type="italic">many,</hi>—various and of divers kinds; numerous and often repeated; and every new miracle confirmed the reality of all that went before. The multitude of his miracles was not only a proof of his unexhausted power, but gave the greater opportunity to examine them; and, if there had been a cheat in them, it was morally impossible but that in some or other of them it would have been discovered; and, being all <hi type="italic">miracles of mercy,</hi> the more there were the more good was done. (2.) The notoriety of them. He wrought these miracles <hi type="italic">before them,</hi> not at a distance, not in a corner, but before many witnesses, appearing to their own eyes. <div eID="gen27885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27886" type="x-p"/> 2. The inefficacy of these means: <hi type="italic">Yet they believed not on him.</hi> They could not gainsay the premises, and yet would not grant the conclusion. Note, The most plentiful and powerful means of conviction will not of themselves work faith in the depraved prejudiced hearts of men. These <hi type="italic">saw,</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">believed not.</hi> <div eID="gen27886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27887" type="x-p"/> 3. The fulfilling of the scripture in this (<reference osisRef="John.12.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">That the saying of Esaias might be fulfilled.</hi> Not that these infidel Jews designed the fulfilling of the scripture (they rather fancied those scriptures which speak of the church's best sons to be fulfilled in themselves), but the event exactly answered the prediction, <hi type="italic">so that (ut for ita ut</hi>) this saying of Esaias was fulfilled. The more improbable any event is, the more does a divine foresight appear in the prediction of it. One could not have imagined that the kingdom of the Messiah, supported with such pregnant proofs, should have met with so much opposition among the Jews, and therefore their unbelief is called a <hi type="italic">marvellous work, and a wonder,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">Isa. xxix. 14</reference>. Christ himself <hi type="italic">marvelled at it,</hi> but it was what Isaiah foretold (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa. liii. 1</reference>), and now it is accomplished. Observe, (1.) The gospel is here called <hi type="italic">their report: Who has believed,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">te akon hemon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">our hearing,</hi> which we have heard from God, and which you have heard from us. Our report is the report that we bring, like the report of a matter of fact, or the report of a solemn resolution in the senate. (2.) It is foretold that a few comparatively of those to whom this report is brought will be persuaded to give credit to it. Many hear it, but few heed it and embrace it: <hi type="italic">Who hath believed it?</hi> Here and there one, but none to speak of; not the wise, not the noble; it is to them but a report which wants confirmation. (3.) It is spoken of as a thing to be greatly lamented that so few believe the report of the gospel. <hi type="italic">Lord</hi> is here prefixed from the LXX., but is not in the Hebrew, and intimates a sorrowful account brought to God by the messengers of the cold entertainment which they and their report had; as <hi type="italic">the servant came, and showed his lord all these things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.14.21">Luke xiv. 21</reference>. (4.) The reason why men believe not the report of the gospel is because <hi type="italic">the arm of the Lord</hi> is not <hi type="italic">revealed</hi> to them, that is, because they do not acquaint themselves with, and submit themselves to, the grace of God; they do not experimentally know the virtue and fellowship of Christ's death and resurrection, in which the arm of the Lord is revealed. They saw Christ's miracles, but did not see the <hi type="italic">arm of the Lord revealed in them.</hi> <div eID="gen27887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27888" type="x-p"/> II. They could not believe, and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they could not <hi type="italic">because Esaias said, He hath blinded their eyes.</hi> This is a hard saying, who can explain it? We are sure that God is infinitely just and merciful, and therefore we cannot think there is in any such an impotency to good, resulting from the counsels of God, as lays them under a fatal necessity of being evil. God dams none by mere sovereignty; yet it is said, <hi type="italic">They could not believe.</hi> St. Austin, coming in course to the exposition of these words, expresses himself with a holy fear of entering upon an enquiry into this mystery. <hi type="italic">Justa sunt judicia ejus, sed occulta—His judgments are just, but hidden.</hi> <div eID="gen27888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27889" type="x-p"/> 1. They <hi type="italic">could not</hi> believe, that is, they <hi type="italic">would not;</hi> they were obstinately resolved in their infidelity; thus Chrysostom and Austin incline to understand it; and the former gives divers instances of scripture of the putting of an impotency to signify the invincible refusal of the will, as <reference osisRef="Gen.37.4">Gen. xxxvii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">They could not speak peaceably to him.</hi> And <reference osisRef="John.7.7">ch. vii. 7</reference>. This is a <hi type="italic">moral</hi> impotency, like that of one that is accustomed to do evil, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.23">Jer. xiii. 23</reference>. But, <div eID="gen27889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27890" type="x-p"/> 2. They could not because Esaias had said, <hi type="italic">He hath blinded their eyes.</hi> Here the difficulty increases; it is certain that God is not the author of sin, and yet, <div eID="gen27890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27891" type="x-p"/> (1.) There is a righteous hand of God sometimes to be acknowledged in the blindness and obstinacy of those who persist in impenitency and unbelief, by which they are justly punished for their former resistance of the divine light and rebellion against the divine law. If God withhold abused grace, and give men over to indulged lusts,—if he permit the evil spirit to do his work on those that resisted the good Spirit,—and if in his providence he lay stumbling-blocks in the way of sinners, which confirm their prejudices, then he <hi type="italic">blinds their eyes,</hi> and <hi type="italic">hardens their hearts,</hi> and these are spiritual judgments, like the giving up of idolatrous Gentiles to <hi type="italic">vile affections,</hi> and degenerate Christians to <hi type="italic">strong delusions.</hi> Observe the method of conversion implied here, and the steps taken in it. [1.] Sinners are brought to <hi type="italic">see with their eyes,</hi> to discern the reality of divine things and to have some knowledge of them. [2.] To <hi type="italic">understand with their heart,</hi> to apply these things to themselves; not only to assent and approve, but to consent and accept. [3.] To <hi type="italic">be converted,</hi> and effectually turned from sin to Christ, from the world and the flesh to God, as their felicity and portion. [4.] Then God will <hi type="italic">heal</hi> them, will justify and sanctify them; will <hi type="italic">pardon</hi> their sins, which are as bleeding wounds, and mortify their corruptions, which are as lurking diseases. Now when God denies his grace nothing of this is done; the alienation of the mind from, and its aversion to, God and the divine life, grow into a rooted and invincible antipathy, and so the case becomes desperate. <div eID="gen27891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27892" type="x-p"/> (2.) Judicial blindness and hardness are in the word of God threatened against those who wilfully persist in wickedness, and were particularly foretold concerning the Jewish church and nation. Known unto God are all his works, and all ours too. Christ knew before who would betray him, and spoke of it, <reference osisRef="John.6.70">ch. vi. 70</reference>. This is a confirmation of the truth of scripture prophecies, and thus even the unbelief of the Jews may help to strengthen our faith. It is also intended for caution to particular persons, to <hi type="italic">beware lest that come upon them which was spoken of in the prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.40">Acts xiii. 40</reference>. <div eID="gen27892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27893" type="x-p"/> (3.) What God has foretold will certainly come to pass, and so, by a necessary consequence, in order of arguing, it might be said that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they <hi type="italic">could not believe,</hi> because God by the prophets had foretold they would not; for such is the knowledge of God that he cannot be deceived in what he foresees, and such his truth that he cannot deceive in what he foretels, so that the scripture cannot be broken. Yet be it observed that the prophecy did not name particular persons; so that it might not be said, "Therefore such a one and such a one could not believe, because Esaias had said so and so;" but it pointed at the body of the Jewish nation, which would persist in their infidelity till their cities were wasted without inhabitants, as it follows (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.11-Isa.6.12">Isa. vi. 11, 12</reference>); yet still reserving a remnant (<reference osisRef="John.12.13">v. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">in it shall be a tenth</hi>), which reserve was sufficient to keep a door of hope open to particular persons; for each one might say, Why may not I be of that remnant? <div eID="gen27893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27894" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The evangelist, having quoted the prophecy, shows (<reference osisRef="John.12.41">v. 41</reference>) that it was intended to look further than the prophet's own days, and that its principal reference was to the days of the Messiah: <hi type="italic">These things said Esaias when he saw his glory, and spoke of him.</hi> 1. We read in the prophecy that this was said to Esaias, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.8-Isa.6.9">Isa. vi. 8, 9</reference>. But here we are told that it was said <hi type="italic">by him</hi> to the purpose. For nothing was said by him as a prophet which was not first said to him; nor was any thing said to him which was not afterwards said by him to those to whom he was sent. See <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>. 2. The vision which the prophet there had of the <hi type="italic">glory of God</hi> is here said to be his <hi type="italic">seeing the glory</hi> of Jesus Christ: He <hi type="italic">saw his glory.</hi> Jesus Christ therefore is equal in power and glory with the Father, and his praises are equally celebrated. Christ had a glory <hi type="italic">before the foundation of the world,</hi> and Esaias saw this. 3. It is said that the prophet there <hi type="italic">spoke of him.</hi> It seems to have been spoken of the prophet himself (for to him the commission and instructions were there given), and yet it is here said to be spoken of Christ, for as all the prophets testified of him so they all typified him. This they spoke of him, that as to many his coming would be not only fruitless, but fatal, a savour of death unto death. It might be objected against his doctrine, If it was from heaven, why did not the Jews believe it? But this is an answer to it; it was not for want of evidence, but because their <hi type="italic">heart was made fat,</hi> and their <hi type="italic">ears were heavy.</hi> It was spoken of Christ, that he should be glorified in the ruin of an unbelieving multitude, as well as in the salvation of a distinguished remnant.
entries.c94be3701d15920df52676950d2efd7242995827: <div eID="gen27894" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cowardice of the Rulers.</title> <div sID="gen27895" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">42</hi> Nevertheless among the chief rulers also many believed on him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess <hi type="italic">him,</hi> lest they should be put out of the synagogue: <hi type="super">43</hi> For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God. <div eID="gen27895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27896" type="x-p"/> Some honour was done to Christ by these rulers: for they <hi type="italic">believed on him,</hi> were convinced that he was sent of God, and received his doctrine as divine; but they did not do him honour enough, for they had not courage to own their faith in him. Many professed more kindness for Christ than really they had; these had more kindness for him than they were willing to profess. See here what a struggle was in these rulers between their convictions and their corruptions. <div eID="gen27896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27897" type="x-p"/> I. See the power of the word in the convictions that many of them were under, who did not wilfully shut their eyes against the light. They <hi type="italic">believed on him</hi> as Nicodemus, received him as a teacher come from God. Note, The truth of the gospel has perhaps a better interest in the consciences of men than we are aware of. Many cannot but approve of that in their hearts which yet outwardly they are shy of. Perhaps these chief rulers were <hi type="italic">true</hi> believers, though very weak, and their faith like smoking flax. Note, It may be, there are more good people than we think there are. Elijah thought he was left alone, when God had seven thousand faithful worshippers in Israel. Some are really better than they seem to be. Their faults are known, but their repentance is not; a man's goodness may be concealed by a <hi type="italic">culpable</hi> yet pardonable weakness, which he himself truly repents of. The <hi type="italic">kingdom of God comes not</hi> in all <hi type="italic">with</hi> a like <hi type="italic">observation;</hi> nor have all who are good the same faculty of appearing to be so. <div eID="gen27897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27898" type="x-p"/> II. See the power of the world in the smothering of these convictions. They believed in Christ, but because of the Pharisees, who had it in their power to do them a diskindness, they durst not confess him for fear of being excommunicated. Observe here, 1. Wherein they failed and were defective; They did not <hi type="italic">confess</hi> Christ. Note, There is cause to question the sincerity of that faith which is either afraid or ashamed to show itself; for those who believe with the heart ought to <hi type="italic">confess with the mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.10.9">Rom. x. 9</reference>. 2. What they feared: being <hi type="italic">put out of the synagogue,</hi> which they thought would be a disgrace and damage to them; as if it would do them any harm to be expelled from a synagogue that had made itself a synagogue of Satan, and from which God was departing. 3. What was at the bottom of this fear: <hi type="italic">They loved the praise of men,</hi> chose it as a more valuable good, and pursued it as a more desirable end, than the <hi type="italic">praise of God;</hi> which was an implicit idolatry, like that (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.25">Rom. i. 25</reference>) of <hi type="italic">worshipping and serving the creature more than the Creator.</hi> They set these two in the scale one against the other, and, having weighed them, they proceeded accordingly. (1.) They set the praise of men in one scale, and considered how good it was to give praise to men, and to pay a deference to the opinion of the Pharisees, and receive praise from men, to be commended by the chief priests and applauded by the people as good sons of the church, the Jewish church; and they would not confess Christ, lest they should thereby derogate from the reputation of the Pharisees, and forfeit their own, and thus hinder their own preferment. And, besides, the followers of Christ were put into an <hi type="italic">ill name,</hi> and were looked upon with contempt, which those who had been used to honour could not bear. Yet perhaps if they had known one another's minds they would have had more courage; but each one thought that if he should declare himself in favour of Christ he should stand alone, and have nobody to back him; whereas, if any one had had resolution to <hi type="italic">break the ice,</hi> he would have had more <hi type="italic">seconds</hi> than he thought of. (2.) They put the praise of God in the other scale. They were sensible that by confessing Christ they should both give praise to God, and have praise from God, that he would be pleased with them, and say, <hi type="italic">Well done;</hi> but, (3.) They gave the preference to the praise of men, and this turned the scale; sense prevailed above faith, and represented it as more desirable to stand right in the opinion of the Pharisees than to be accepted of God. Note, Love of the praise of men is a very great prejudice to the power and practice of religion and godliness. Many come short of the glory of God by having a regard to the applause of men, and a value for that. Love of the praise of men, as a by-end in that which is good, will make a man a hypocrite when religion is in fashion and credit is to be got by it; and love of the praise of men, as a base principle in that which is evil, will make a man an apostate when religion is in disgrace, and credit is to be lost for it, as here. See <reference osisRef="Rom.2.29">Rom. ii. 29</reference>.
entries.dc8e20cd2b2092b582e420dd5aad8dd6ff7e310e: <div eID="gen27898" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Last Discourse with the Jews.</title> <div sID="gen27899" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">44</hi> Jesus cried and said, He that believeth on me, believeth not on me, but on him that sent me. <hi type="super">45</hi> And he that seeth me seeth him that sent me. <hi type="super">46</hi> I am come a light into the world, that whosoever believeth on me should not abide in darkness. <hi type="super">47</hi> And if any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not: for I came not to judge the world, but to save the world. <hi type="super">48</hi> He that rejecteth me, and receiveth not my words, hath one that judgeth him: the word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day. <hi type="super">49</hi> For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak. <hi type="super">50</hi> And I know that his commandment is life everlasting: whatsoever I speak therefore, even as the Father said unto me, so I speak. <div eID="gen27899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27900" type="x-p"/> We have here the honour Christ not assumed, but asserted, to himself, in the account he gave of his mission and his errand into the world. Probably this discourse was not at the same time with that before (for them <hi type="italic">he departed,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.36">v. 36</reference>), but some time after, when he made another public appearance; and, as this evangelist records it, it was Christ's farewell sermon to the Jews, and his last public discourse; all that follows was private with his disciples. Now observe how our Lord Jesus delivered this parting word: he <hi type="italic">cried and said. Doth not wisdom cry</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.1">Prov. viii. 1</reference>), cry <hi type="italic">without?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Prov. i. 20</reference>. The raising of his voice and crying intimate, 1. His boldness in speaking. Though they had not courage openly to profess faith in his doctrine, he had courage openly to publish it; if they were ashamed of it, he was not, but set his face as a flint, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">Isa. l. 7</reference>. 2. His earnestness in speaking. He cried as one that was serious and importunate, and in good earnest in what he said, and was willing to impart to them, not only the gospel of God, but <hi type="italic">even his own soul.</hi> 3. It denotes his desire that all might take notice of it. This being the last time of the publication of his gospel by himself in person, he makes proclamation, "Whoever will hear me, let them come now." Now what is the conclusion of the whole matter, this closing summary of all Christ's discourses? It is much like that of Moses (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.15">Deut. xxx. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">See, I have set before you life and death.</hi> So Christ here takes leave of the temple, with a solemn declaration of three things:— <div eID="gen27900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27901" type="x-p"/> I. The privileges and dignities of those that believe; this gives great encouragement to us to believe in Christ and to profess that faith. It is a thing of such a nature that we need not be shy either of doing it or of owning it; for, <div eID="gen27901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27902" type="x-p"/> 1. By believing in Christ we are brought into an <hi type="italic">honourable acquaintance with God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.12.44-John.12.45">v. 44, 45</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that believes on me,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">sees me, believes on him that sent me,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">sees him.</hi> He that believes on Christ, (1.) He does not believe in a mere man, such a one as he seemed to be, and was generally taken to be, but he believes in one that is the Son of God and equal in power and glory with the Father. Or rather, (2.) His faith does not terminate in Christ, but through him it is carried out to the Father, that sent him, to whom, as our end, we come by Christ as our way. The doctrine of Christ is believed and received as the truth of God. The rest of a believing soul is in God through Christ as Mediator; for its resignation to Christ is in order to being presented to God. Christianity is made up, not of philosophy nor politics, but pure divinity. This is illustrated, <reference osisRef="John.12.45">v. 45</reference>. He that <hi type="italic">sees me</hi> (which is the same with <hi type="italic">believing</hi> in him, for faith is the eye of the soul) <hi type="italic">sees him that sent me;</hi> in getting an acquaintance with Christ, we come to the knowledge of God. For, [1.] God makes himself known in the face of Christ (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>), who is the express image of his person, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb. i. 3</reference>. [2.] All that have a believing sight of Christ are led by him to the knowledge of God, whom Christ has revealed to us by his word and Spirit. Christ, as God, was the image of his Father's person; but Christ, as Mediator, was his Father's representative in his relation to man, the divine light, law, and love, being communicated to us in and through him; so that in seeing him (that is, in eying him as our Saviour, Prince, and Lord, in the right of redemption), we see and eye the Father as our owner, ruler, and benefactor, in the right of creation: for God is pleased to deal with fallen man by proxy. <div eID="gen27902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27903" type="x-p"/> 2. We are hereby brought into a comfortable enjoyment of ourselves (<reference osisRef="John.12.46">v. 46</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am come a light into the world, that whoever believes in me,</hi> Jew or Gentile, <hi type="italic">should not abide in darkness.</hi> Observe, (1.) The character of Christ: <hi type="italic">I am come a light into the world,</hi> to be a light to it. This implies that he had a being, and a being as light, before he came into the world, as the sun is before it rises; the prophets and apostles were made lights to the world, but it was Christ only that came a light into this world, having before been a glorious light in the upper world, <reference osisRef="John.3.19">ch. iii. 19</reference>. (2.) The comfort of Christians: They <hi type="italic">do not abide in darkness.</hi> [1.] They do not continue in that dark condition in which they were by nature; they are <hi type="italic">light in the Lord.</hi> They are without any true comfort, or joy, or hope, but do not continue in that condition; light is sown for them. [2.] Whatever darkness of affliction, disquietment, or fear, they may afterwards be in, provision is made that they may not long abide in it. [3.] They are delivered from that darkness which is perpetual, and which <hi type="italic">abideth for ever,</hi> that utter darkness where there is not the least gleam of light nor hope of it. <div eID="gen27903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27904" type="x-p"/> II. The peril and danger of those that believe not, which gives fair warning to take heed of persisting in unbelief (<reference osisRef="John.12.47-John.12.48">v. 47, 48</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If any man hear my words, and believe not, I judge him not,</hi> not I only, or not now, lest I should be looked upon as unfair in being judge in my own cause; yet let not infidelity think therefore to go unpunished, <hi type="italic">though I judge him not, there is one that judgeth him.</hi>" So that we have here the doom of unbelief. Observe, <div eID="gen27904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27905" type="x-p"/> 1. Who they are whose unbelief is here condemned: those who <hi type="italic">hear Christ's words</hi> and yet <hi type="italic">believe them not.</hi> Those shall not be condemned for their infidelity that never had, nor could have, the gospel; every man shall be judged according to the dispensation of light he was under: <hi type="italic">Those that have sinned without law shall be judged without law.</hi> But those that have heard, or might have heard, and would not, lie open to this doom. <div eID="gen27905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27906" type="x-p"/> 2. What is the constructive malignity of their unbelief: not receiving Christ's word; it is interpreted (<reference osisRef="John.12.48">v. 48</reference>) a <hi type="italic">rejecting</hi> of Christ, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ho atheton eme</hi></hi>. It denotes a rejection with scorn and contempt. Where the banner of the gospel is displayed, no neutrality is admitted; every man is either a subject or an enemy. <div eID="gen27906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27907" type="x-p"/> 3. The wonderful patience and forbearance of our Lord Jesus, exercised towards those who slighted him when he was come here upon earth: <hi type="italic">I judge him not,</hi> not now. Note, Christ was not quick or hasty to take advantage against those who refused the first offers of his grace, but continued waiting to be gracious. He did not strike those dumb or dead who contradicted him, never made intercession against Israel, as Elias did; though he had authority to judge, he suspended the execution of it, because he had work of another nature to do first, and that was to <hi type="italic">save the world.</hi> (1.) To save effectually those that were given him before he came to judge the degenerate body of mankind. (2.) To offer salvation to all the world, and thus far to save them that it is their own fault if they be not saved. He was to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself. Now the executing of the power of a judge was not congruous with that undertaking, <reference osisRef="Acts.8.33">Acts viii. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">In his humiliation his judgment was taken away,</hi> it was suspended for a time. <div eID="gen27907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27908" type="x-p"/> 4. The certain and unavoidable judgment of unbelievers at the great day, the day of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God: unbelief will certainly be a damning sin. Some think when Christ saith, <hi type="italic">I judge no man,</hi> he means that they are <hi type="italic">condemned already.</hi> There needs no process, they are <hi type="italic">self-judged;</hi> no execution, they are <hi type="italic">self-ruined;</hi> judgment goes against them of course, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.3">Heb. ii. 3</reference>. Christ needs not appear against them as their accuser, they are miserable if he do not appear for them as their advocate; however, he tells them plainly when and where they will be reckoned with. (1.) There is <hi type="italic">one that judgeth them.</hi> Nothing is more dreadful than abused patience, and grace trampled on; though for awhile <hi type="italic">mercy rejoiceth against judgment,</hi> yet there will be <hi type="italic">judgment without mercy.</hi> (2.) Their final judgment is reserved to the <hi type="italic">last day;</hi> to that day of judgment Christ here binds over all unbelievers, to answer then for all the contempts they have put upon him. Divine justice has <hi type="italic">appointed a day,</hi> and adjourns the sentence to that day, as <reference osisRef="Matt.26.64">Matt. xxvi. 64</reference>. (3.) The word of Christ will judge them then: <hi type="italic">The words that I have spoken,</hi> how light soever you have made of them, <hi type="italic">the same shall judge</hi> the unbeliever <hi type="italic">in the last day;</hi> as the apostles, the preachers of Christ's word, are said to judge, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.30">Luke xxii. 30</reference>. Christ's words will judge unbelievers two ways:—[1.] As the evidence of their crime, they will convict them. Every word Christ spoke, every sermon, every argument, every kind offer, will be produced as a testimony against those who slighted all he said. [2.] As the rule of their doom, they will condemn them; they shall be judged according to the tenour of that covenant which Christ procured and published. That word of Christ, <hi type="italic">He that believes not shall be damned,</hi> will judge all unbelievers to eternal ruin; and there are <hi type="italic">many such like words.</hi> <div eID="gen27908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27909" type="x-p"/> III. A solemn declaration of the authority Christ had to demand our faith, and require us to receive his doctrine upon pain of damnation, <reference osisRef="John.12.49-John.12.50">v. 49, 50</reference>, where observe, <div eID="gen27909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27910" type="x-p"/> 1. The commission which our Lord Jesus received from the Father to deliver his doctrine to the world (<reference osisRef="John.12.49">v. 49</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have not spoken myself,</hi> as a mere man, much less as a common man; <hi type="italic">but the Father gave me a commandment what I should say.</hi> This is the same with what he said <reference osisRef="John.7.16">ch. vii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">My doctrine is,</hi> (1.) <hi type="italic">Not mine,</hi> for <hi type="italic">I have not spoken of myself.</hi> Christ, as <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> did not speak that which was of human contrivance or composure; as Son of God, he did not act separately, or by himself alone, but what he said was the result of the counsels of peace; as Mediator, his coming into the world was voluntary, and with his full consent, but not arbitrary, and of his own head. But, (2.) It was his that sent him. God the Father gave him, [1.] His commission. God sent him as his agent and plenipotentiary, to concert matters between him and man, to set a treaty of peace on foot, and to settle the articles. [2.] His instructions, here called a <hi type="italic">commandment,</hi> for they were like those given to an ambassador, directing him not only what he may say, but what he must say. The messenger of the covenant was entrusted with an errand which he must deliver. Note, Our Lord Jesus learned obedience himself, before he taught it to us, though he was a Son. <hi type="italic">The Lord God commanded</hi> the first Adam, and he by his disobedience ruined us; he commanded the second Adam, and he by his obedience saved us. God commanded him what he should <hi type="italic">say</hi> and what he should <hi type="italic">speak,</hi> two words signifying the same thing, to denote that every word was divine. The Old-Testament prophets sometimes spoke of themselves; but Christ spoke by the Spirit at all times. Some make this distinction: He was directed what he should say in his set sermons, and what he should speak in his familiar discourses. Others this: He was directed what he should say in his preaching now, and what he should speak in his judging at the last day; for he had commission and instruction for both. <div eID="gen27910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27911" type="x-p"/> 2. The scope, design, and tendency of this commission: <hi type="italic">I know that his commandment is life everlasting,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.50">v. 50</reference>. The commission given to Christ had a reference to the everlasting state of the children of men, and was in order to their everlasting life and happiness in that state: the instructions given to Christ as a prophet were to reveal eternal life (<reference osisRef="1John.5.11">1 John v. 11</reference>); the power, given to Christ as a king was to give eternal life, <reference osisRef="John.17.2">ch. xvii. 2</reference>. Thus the command given him was life everlasting. This Christ says he knew: "I know it is so," which intimates how cheerfully and with what assurance Christ pursued his undertaking, knowing very well that he went upon a good errand, and that which would bring forth fruit unto life eternal. It intimates likewise how justly those will perish who reject Christ and his word. Those who disobey Christ despise everlasting life, and renounce it; so that not only Christ's words will judge them, but even their own; so shall their doom be, themselves have decided it; and who can except against it? <div eID="gen27911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27912" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's exact observance of the commission and instructions given him, and his steady acting in pursuance of them: <hi type="italic">Whatsoever I speak,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">as the Father said unto me.</hi> Christ was intimately acquainted with the counsels of God, and was faithful in discovering so much of them to the children of men as it was agreed should be discovered, and <hi type="italic">kept back nothing that was profitable.</hi> As the faithful witness delivers souls, so did he, and spoke the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Note, (1.) This is a great encouragement to faith; the sayings of Christ, rightly understood, are what we may venture our souls upon. (2.) It is a great example of obedience. Christ said as he was bidden, and so must we, communicated what the Father had said to him, and so must we. See <reference osisRef="Acts.4.20">Acts iv. 20</reference>. In the midst of all the respect paid to him, this is the honour he values himself upon, that what the Father had said to him that he spoke, and in the manner as he was directed so he spoke. This was his glory, that, as a Son, he was faithful to him that appointed him; and, by an unfeigned belief of every word of Christ, and an entire subjection of soul to it, we must give him the glory due to his name.  <chapter eID="John.12"/> <div eID="gen27912" type="x-p"/>

entries.a8856e5b0011b0f39b2b9458f9f202ac90c83752: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15250"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.12.1-John.12.11">Joh 12:1-11</reference>. The Anointing at Bethany.</title> <div sID="gen29325" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.26.6-Matt.26.13">Mt 26:6-13</reference>).<div eID="gen29325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15250"/><hi type="bold">1-8. six days before the passover--</hi>that is, on the sixth day before it; probably after sunset on Friday evening, or the commencement of the Jewish sabbath preceding the passover. <div eID="gen29326" type="x-p"/>
entries.f970c5ec25014d2dc26fc42ecd86633be399be7e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15258"/><div sID="gen29350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15258"/><hi type="bold">9-11. Crowds of the Jerusalem Jews hastened to Bethany, not so much to see Jesus, whom they knew to be there, as to see dead Lazarus alive; and this, issuing in their accession to Christ, led to a plot against the life of Lazarus also, as the only means of arresting the triumphs of Jesus (see <reference osisRef="John.12.19">Joh 12:19</reference>)--</hi>to such a pitch had these chief priests come of diabolical determination to shut out the light from themselves, and quench it from the earth!<div eID="gen29350" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.12.12-John.12.19">Joh 12:12-19</reference>. Christ's Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen29351" type="x-p"/> (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.21.1-Matt.21.9">Mt 21:1-9</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Luke.19.29-Luke.19.36">Lu 19:29-36</reference>). <div eID="gen29351" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebf39c4bfdc342856b35e9a77beb37376912630f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15259"/><div sID="gen29352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15259"/><hi type="bold">12. On the next day--</hi>the Lord's day, or Sunday (see on <reference osisRef="John.12.1">Joh 12:1</reference>); the tenth day of the Jewish month Nisan, on which the paschal lamb was set apart to be "kept up until the fourteenth day of the same month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel were to kill it in the evening" (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.3">Ex 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.6">6</reference>). Even so, from the day of this solemn entry into Jerusalem, "Christ our Passover" was virtually set apart to be "sacrificed for us" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1Co 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen29352" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f90d2563c43009d6b47c7ff69b95ae1d128dcf8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15260"/><div sID="gen29353" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15260"/><hi type="bold">16. when Jesus was glorified, then remembered they that these things were written of him, &c.--</hi>The Spirit, descending on them from the glorified Saviour at Pentecost, opened their eyes suddenly to the true sense of the Old Testament, brought vividly to their recollection this and other Messianic predictions, and to their unspeakable astonishment showed them that they, and all the actors in these scenes, had been unconsciously fulfilling those predictions. <div eID="gen29353" type="x-p"/>
entries.81a559e38058eb0f5c59d746975b522eb42abac9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15261"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.12.20-John.12.36">Joh 12:20-36</reference>. Some Greeks Desire to See Jesus--The Discourse and Scene Thereupon.</title> <div sID="gen29354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15261"/><hi type="bold">20-22. Greeks--</hi>Not Grecian Jews, but Greek proselytes to the Jewish faith, who were wont to attend the annual festivals, particularly this primary one, the Passover.<div eID="gen29354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The same came therefore to Philip ... of Bethsaida--</hi>possibly as being from the same quarter.<div eID="gen29355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, Sir, we would see Jesus--</hi>certainly in a far better sense than Zaccheus (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.3">Lu 19:3</reference>). Perhaps He was then in that part of the temple court to which Gentile proselytes had no access. "These men from the west represent, at the end of Christ's life, what the wise men from the east represented at its beginning; but those come to the cross of the King, even as these to His manger" [Stier]. <div eID="gen29356" type="x-p"/>
entries.b77f1d463ec71898c8ca3f1f3e7cb67db9e84de9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15263"/><div sID="gen29359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15263"/><hi type="bold">23-26. Jesus answered them, The hour is come that the Son of man should be glorified--</hi>that is, They would see Jesus, would they? Yet a little moment, and they shall see Him so as now they dream not of. The middle wall of partition that keeps them out from the commonwealth of Israel is on the eve of breaking down, "and I, if I be lifted up from the earth, shall draw all men unto Me"; I see them "flying as a cloud, and as doves to their cotes"--a glorious event that will be for the Son of man, by which this is to be brought about. It is His death He thus sublimely and delicately alluded to. Lost in the scenes of triumph which this desire of the Greeks to see Him called up before His view, He gives no direct answer to their petition for an interview, but sees the cross which was to bring them gilded with glory. <div eID="gen29359" type="x-p"/>
entries.a868f266a8f3cb58e6896d6f4191c4b7dee21f65: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15267"/><div sID="gen29363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15267"/><hi type="bold">27-28. Now is my soul troubled--</hi>He means at the prospect of His death, just alluded to. Strange view of the Cross this, immediately after representing it as the hour of His glory! (<reference osisRef="John.12.23">Joh 12:23</reference>). But the two views naturally meet, and blend into one. It was the Greeks, one might say, that troubled Him.
